q: What does Descartes' Latin dictum "Cogito, ergo sum" mean in English?
explain: Descartes treated the cogito as the one statement that survives his method of doubt, making it a foundation for certain knowledge.

sources.title: Cogito, ergo sum | Britannica
sources.quote: Latin: “I think, therefore I am” ... Cogito, ergo sum , dictum coined by the French mathematician and philosopher René Descartes in his Discourse on Method (1637) as a first step in demonstrating the attainability of certain knowledge. It is the only statement to survive the test of his methodic doubt.

sources.title: Descartes’ Epistemology (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: As the canonical formulation has it, I think therefore I am (Latin: cogito ergo sum ; French: je pense , donc je suis )

q: In which 1637 work did Descartes first state "I think, therefore I am"?
explain: The phrase appeared in French (je pense, donc je suis) in the Discourse on Method (1637); the Meditations on First Philosophy (1641) argued the same point without the canonical wording.

sources.title: Cogito, ergo sum | Britannica
sources.quote: Cogito, ergo sum , dictum coined by the French mathematician and philosopher René Descartes in his Discourse on Method (1637) as a first step in demonstrating the attainability of certain knowledge.

sources.title: Cogito Ergo Sum - The Cambridge Descartes Lexicon
sources.quote: The “canonical” formulation (as I shall call it) includes an explicit inference – “I am thinking, therefore [ ergo ] I exist.” This version appears in two of the works: the Discourse (1637) ( je pense, donc je suis ), and the Principles (1644) ( ego cogito, ergo sum ).

q: Which English philosopher wrote Leviathan, first published in 1651?
explain: Leviathan argues that political authority is justified by a hypothetical social contract that vests a sovereign with responsibility for everyone's safety.

sources.title: Leviathan | Thomas Hobbes | Britannica
sources.quote: Leviathan , magnum opus of the early-modern English political philosopher, ethicist, metaphysician, and scientist Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679). First published in 1651

sources.title: How did Thomas Hobbes describe the state of nature? | Britannica
sources.quote: individuals rationally agree to relinquish their natural rights and transfer their self-sovereignty to a sovereign —or Leviathan —in exchange for physical safety and the establishment of peace.

q: Hobbes described life without peace as "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and" what?
explain: The line comes from Leviathan, Chapter XIII, describing life in the state of nature without a common authority.

sources.title: Leviathan | Thomas Hobbes | Britannica
sources.quote: Without peace, he observed, humans live in “continual fear, and danger of violent death,” and what life they have is “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short” ( Leviathan , Chapter XIII).

sources.title: How did Thomas Hobbes describe the state of nature? | Britannica
sources.quote: Consequently, Hobbes described human life in this state as "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short".

q: What Latin term for a "blank slate" describes Locke's view of the mind before experience?
explain: In An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), Locke compared the mind to "white paper, void of all characters," with knowledge derived from experience.

sources.title: Tabula rasa | Britannica
sources.quote: the English empiricist John Locke , in An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), argued for the mind’s initial resemblance to “white paper, void of all characters,” with “all the materials of reason and knowledge” derived from experience.

sources.title: John Locke (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Locke holds that the mind is a tabula rasa or blank sheet until experience in the form of sensation and reflection provide the basic materials—simple ideas—out of which most of our more complex knowledge is constructed.

q: Which Scottish philosopher gave the classic formulation of the problem of induction?
explain: Hume noted that inferences from the observed to the unobserved rely on the rationally unfounded premise that the future will resemble the past.

sources.title: Problem of induction | Britannica
sources.quote: It was given its classic formulation by the Scottish philosopher David Hume (1711–76), who noted that all such inferences rely, directly or indirectly, on the rationally unfounded premise that the future will resemble the past.

sources.title: The Problem of Induction (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: The original source of what has become known as the “problem of induction” is in Book 1, part iii, section 6 of A Treatise of Human Nature by David Hume, published in 1739 (Hume 1739).

q: In which work, published in 1739, did Hume first present the problem of induction?
explain: Hume later gave a shorter version of the argument in An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748).

sources.title: The Problem of Induction (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: The original source of what has become known as the “problem of induction” is in Book 1, part iii, section 6 of A Treatise of Human Nature by David Hume, published in 1739 (Hume 1739). In 1748, Hume gave a shorter version of the argument in Section iv of An enquiry concerning human understanding (Hume 1748).

sources.title: David Hume (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Books 1 and 2 of the Treatise were published anonymously in 1739, with Book 3 (as well as a similarly anonymous “Abstract” of the first two books) following a year later in 1740.

q: What did Kant call his supreme moral principle, e.g. "Act only on that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law"?
explain: It is categorical because it applies unconditionally to all rational agents, regardless of their desires or goals.

sources.title: Immanuel Kant and the three critiques | Britannica
sources.quote: Kant’s ethics ... was based on the principle known as the “categorical imperative,” one formulation of which is, “Act only on that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.”

sources.title: Kant’s Moral Philosophy (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) argued that the supreme principle of morality is a principle of rationality that he dubbed the “Categorical Imperative” (CI).

q: What is the full title of Kant's first Critique, published in 1781?
wrong: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
explain: Its first edition appeared in 1781 and a revised second edition in 1787; the Critique of Practical Reason (1788) and Critique of Judgment (1790) followed.

sources.title: Immanuel Kant and the three critiques | Britannica
sources.quote: His Critique of Pure Reason (1781) discusses the nature of knowledge in mathematics and physics and demonstrates the impossibility of knowledge in metaphysics as it was traditionally conceived.

sources.title: Immanuel Kant (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: especially in his three Critiques: the Critique of Pure Reason (1781, 1787), the Critique of Practical Reason (1788), and the Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790)

q: In which Prussian city was Immanuel Kant born, and where did he teach?
explain: Königsberg was then the capital of East Prussia; today it is Kaliningrad, part of Russia.

sources.title: Immanuel Kant and the three critiques | Britannica
sources.quote: Immanuel Kant , (born April 22, 1724, Königsberg, Prussia—died Feb. 12, 1804, Königsberg), German philosopher ... he studied at the university in Königsberg and taught there

sources.title: Immanuel Kant (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Immanuel Kant was born April 22, 1724 in Königsberg, near the southeastern shore of the Baltic Sea. Today Königsberg has been renamed Kaliningrad and is part of Russia.

q: Which philosopher, the earliest expounder of utilitarianism, held that legislation should aim at "the greatest happiness of the greatest number"?
explain: Bentham argued that mankind is governed by two sovereign motives, pain and pleasure.

sources.title: Jeremy Bentham summary | Britannica
sources.quote: British moral philosopher and legal theorist, the earliest expounder of utilitarianism ... The object of all legislation, therefore, must be the “greatest happiness of the greatest number”

sources.title: Bentham, Jeremy | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: Specifically, then, what is morally obligatory is that which produces the greatest amount of happiness for the greatest number of people, happiness being determined by reference to the presence of pleasure and the absence of pain.

q: What is the name of Bentham's method for calculating amounts of pleasure and pain?
explain: It weighs dimensions such as intensity, duration, certainty and propinquity; Bentham did not himself use the term, which became its common name.

sources.title: Jeremy Bentham | Britannica
sources.quote: his “felicific calculus,” a method for calculating amounts of happiness, as even his warmest admirers have admitted, cannot be used.

sources.title: Jeremy Bentham (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Though Bentham did not use this terminology, the calculus he devised—commonly known as the “felicific calculus”—describes the elements or dimensions of the value of a pain or pleasure. To an individual the value of a pain or pleasure will be more or less according to its “intensity”, “duration”, “certainty or uncertainty”, and its “propinquity or remoteness”.

q: What is the name of Mill's principle in On Liberty that power may be exercised over an individual only to prevent harm to others?
explain: Mill wrote that a person's own good, physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant for compelling him.

sources.title: Mill, John Stuart | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: This “one very simple principle”—often called the “harm principle”—entails that: ... That the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant.

sources.title: Mill’s Moral and Political Philosophy (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Whereas Mill appears to reject the regulation of mere offense, the harm principle appears to be the one justification he recognizes for restricting liberty.

q: Which philosopher wrote the 1861 book Utilitarianism?
explain: Utilitarianism (1861) and On Liberty (1859) are Mill's two best-known works.

sources.title: Mill’s Moral and Political Philosophy (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: We will concentrate on his two most popular and best known works, Utilitarianism (1861, cited as U ) and On Liberty (1859, cited as OL )

sources.title: Jeremy Bentham (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: As is well known, while adhering to the basic Benthamic analysis of motives, in Utilitarianism (1861) J. S.

q: Which German philosopher famously proclaimed that "God is dead"?
explain: The pronouncement appears in The Gay Science and in Thus Spoke Zarathustra; it claims that belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable, not simply that atheism is true.

sources.title: Thus Spake Zarathustra | Britannica
sources.quote: It is this work in which Nietzsche made his famous (and much misconstrued) statement that “God is dead”

sources.title: Friedrich Nietzsche (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: he launches the famous, aggressive and paradoxical pronouncement that “God is dead” ( GS 108, 125, 343). The idea is not so much that atheism is true ... but instead that because “the belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable”

q: What German term, often translated "superman" or "overman", did Nietzsche present in Thus Spoke Zarathustra?
explain: Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883–85) also introduced the "will to power" and contains the statement "God is dead."

sources.title: Thus Spake Zarathustra | Britannica
sources.quote: It is this work in which Nietzsche made his famous (and much misconstrued) statement that “God is dead” and in which he presented some of the most influential and well-known (and likewise misunderstood) ideas of his philosophy, including those of the Übermensch (“superman”) and the “will to power.”

sources.title: Nietzsche’s Übermensch: A Hero of Our Time? | Philosophy Now
sources.quote: The term Übermensch , often translated as Superman or Overman, was not invented by Nietzsche.

q: Which Danish philosopher is generally considered the father of existentialism?
explain: Kierkegaard (1813–1855) emphasized individual existence and concepts such as authenticity, commitment, anxiety and dread; many of his works were pseudonymous.

sources.title: Søren Kierkegaard | Britannica
sources.quote: For his emphasis on individual existence ... and for his invocation of the associated concepts of authenticity, commitment, responsibility, anxiety, and dread, Søren Kierkegaard is generally considered the father of existentialism .

sources.title: Existentialism | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: Kierkegaard was many things: philosopher, religious writer, satirist, psychologist, journalist, literary critic and generally considered the ‘father’ of existentialism.

q: Which French philosopher coined the existentialist adage "existence precedes essence"?
explain: Sartre called it "the first principle of existentialism": humans first exist and only afterwards define themselves through their choices.

sources.title: Existentialism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Sartre will later repackage this line with the pithy adage, “existence precedes essence” (1946 [2001, 292]).

sources.title: Jean-Paul Sartre | Britannica
sources.quote: Jean-Paul Sartre published his first novel, Nausea , in 1938. The novel stemmed from his belief that “existence precedes essence.”

q: Which French existentialist declined the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature?
explain: Sartre said a writer should not allow himself to be turned into an institution, and he had declined other official honours too.

sources.title: Jean-Paul Sartre | Britannica
sources.quote: In 1964 he declined the Nobel Prize for Literature, which had been awarded to him “for his work which, rich in ideas and filled with the spirit of freedom and the quest for truth, has exerted a far-reaching influence on our age.”

sources.title: The Nobel Prize in Literature 1964 - NobelPrize.org
sources.quote: The Nobel Prize in Literature 1964 was awarded to Jean-Paul Sartre ... Jean-Paul Sartre declined the Nobel Prize.

q: Which figure from Greek myth did Camus use as a metaphor for the human struggle against the absurd?
explain: In The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), Sisyphus is condemned to roll a boulder up a hill forever; Camus argues one should accept the absurd and rebel by embracing the struggle.

sources.title: The Myth of Sisyphus | Britannica
sources.quote: Camus uses the Greek legend of Sisyphus , who is condemned by the gods for eternity to repeatedly roll a boulder up a hill only to have it roll down again once he got it to the top, as a metaphor for the individual’s persistent struggle against the essential absurdity of life.

sources.title: Existentialism | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: In The Myth of Sisyphus Camus tells the story of the mythical Sisyphus who was condemned by the Gods to ceaselessly roll a rock to the top of a mountain and then have to let it fall back again of its own weight.

q: Which Wittgenstein work, published in German in 1921, was the only philosophy book he published in his lifetime?
explain: The Tractatus set out logical atomism and the "picture theory of meaning"; its English edition appeared in 1922.

sources.title: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus | Britannica
sources.quote: It was published in German (as Logisch-philosophische Abhandlung ) in 1921 and in English in 1922.

sources.title: Wittgenstein, Ludwig | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: This work culminated in the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus , the only philosophy book that Wittgenstein published during his lifetime.

sources.title: Ludwig Wittgenstein (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus , always referred to by Wittgenstein as ‘Logisch-Philosophische Abhandlung’, was first published in German in 1921 and then translated ... and published in English in 1922.

q: In which posthumously published work did Wittgenstein develop the concept of "language-games"?
explain: Philosophical Investigations was published in 1953, after his death, and helped inspire ordinary language philosophy.

sources.title: Ludwig Wittgenstein (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Philosophical Investigations ( PI ) was published posthumously in 1953. ... Throughout the Philosophical Investigations , Wittgenstein returns, again and again, to the concept of language-games to make clear his lines of thought concerning language.

sources.title: Wittgenstein, Ludwig | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: Wittgenstein’s later work, principally his Philosophical Investigations , shares this concern with logic and language , but takes a different, less technical, approach to philosophical problems. This book helped to inspire so-called ordinary language philosophy .

q: Which British philosopher first posed the trolley problem, in a 1967 essay?
explain: Foot used it in "The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of Double Effect" (1967); Judith Jarvis Thomson later named it "the trolley problem" (1976).

sources.title: Trolley problem | Britannica
sources.quote: The trolley problem originated in a 1967 essay by the British philosopher Philippa Foot ... The trolley problem, as it came to be known, was first identified as such by the American philosopher Judith Jarvis Thomson, whose essay “Killing, Letting Die, and the Trolley Problem” (1976) spawned a vast academic literature on the topic.

sources.title: Philippa Foot (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: In “The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of Double Effect” (1967), Foot introduces a related case that has since become the subject of extensive discussion: a runaway trolley is headed toward five people who will be killed, but it can be diverted onto a track on which there is only one person

q: Which ancient writer recorded the Ship of Theseus puzzle in his Life of Theseus?
explain: Plutarch says the Athenians replaced the ship's decayed planks with new timber, so philosophers debated whether it remained the same ship.

sources.title: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 23 — Lexundria
sources.quote: They took away the old timbers from time to time, and put new and sound ones in their places, so that the vessel became standing illustration for the philosophers in the mooted question of growth, some declaring that it remained the same, others that it was not the same vessel.

sources.title: Ship of Theseus – Introduction to Philosophy
sources.quote: The paradox is most notably recorded by Plutarch in Life of Theseus from the late first century. Plutarch asked whether a ship that had been restored by replacing every single wooden part remained the same ship.

q: Which medieval philosopher is the principle "plurality should not be posited without necessity" named after?
explain: Occam's razor favours explanations that posit fewer entities; Ockham was not the first to state the idea, but it bears his name.
hook: The razor shaves off unneeded assumptions.

sources.title: Occam’s razor | Britannica
sources.quote: Occam’s razor , principle stated by the Scholastic philosopher William of Ockham (1285–1347/49) that pluralitas non est ponenda sine necessitate , “plurality should not be posited without necessity.”

sources.title: William of Ockham (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Indeed, the principle known as “Ockham’s Razor” is named after him.

q: In which work did Blaise Pascal present his wager?
explain: Pascal's Pensées (1657–58) used early decision-theory reasoning to argue that believing in God is the rational bet.

sources.title: Pascal’s wager | Britannica
sources.quote: Pascal’s wager , practical argument for belief in God formulated by French mathematician and philosopher Blaise Pascal . In his Pensées (1657–58), Pascal applied elements of game theory to show that belief in the Christian religion is rational.

sources.title: Pascal’s Wager (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: “Pascal’s Wager” is the name given to an argument due to Blaise Pascal for believing, or for at least taking steps to believe, in God. The name is somewhat misleading, for in a single section of his Pensées , Pascal apparently presents four such arguments

q: Pascal's wager is an argument for believing in what?
explain: Pascal argued that if God exists, the believer gains everything, while if God does not exist, the believer loses relatively little.
hook: "If you gain, you gain all; if you lose, you lose nothing."

sources.title: Pascal’s wager | Britannica
sources.quote: Pascal’s wager , practical argument for belief in God formulated by French mathematician and philosopher Blaise Pascal . ... “If you gain, you gain all; if you lose, you lose nothing. Wager, then, without hesitation that He is.”

sources.title: Pascal’s Wager (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: “Pascal’s Wager” is the name given to an argument due to Blaise Pascal for believing, or for at least taking steps to believe, in God.
